Why I stopped using a bundler for small sites

Published 18 January 2026

For years every side project of mine started the same way: install a bundler, copy a config from the last repository, and spend an evening fighting plugins before writing a single line of the thing I actually wanted to build.

The moment it stopped making sense

Browsers ship modules natively now. For a site that is a few hundred lines of JavaScript and some CSS, the build step buys almost nothing and costs a config file, a lockfile, and a class of errors that only appear in production.

What I do instead

I serve source files directly, keep dependencies to a handful of small modules, and add a build step only once measurements say the payload hurts. In practice that threshold arrives far later than habit suggests.

What I gave up

Tree shaking and minification, mostly. On a site with three dependencies the difference was eleven kilobytes, which is less than the hero image I had already been careless about for two years.

When I still reach for a bundler

Anything with a component framework, anything with more than a dozen modules, and anything a team maintains. The tooling earns its keep the moment more than one person has to reason about the dependency graph.
